title: Dragons' Den IP Blog - Series 23 Episode 12

content.content: As someone who enjoys cooking, this week's episode of Dragons' Den was certainly a culinary delight, with a whole mix of intellectual property (IP) ingredients in the pot. This week Peter Jones, Steven Bartlett, Deborah Meaden and Touker Suleyman were joined by guest Dragon, Susie Ma.
From Cumbria with amore

First into the Den was husband and wife team, Imogen and Matt, co-founders of ‘Northern Pasta Co’, a business making pasta from regeneratively grown British spelt. The pair make the pasta themselves using traditional methods in Cumbria. They were looking for a £50k investment in return for 5% of their business.
Deborah kicked off the questioning, and it wasn't long before the brand of the business was discussed, asking "why Northern Pasta Co?".

A 'brand' is how a business sets itself apart from others, with its name, logo and even values, giving customers a way to recognise it. After doing a quick search on the trade marks register, I could see that their business has registered a trade mark for Northern Pasta Co.

A registered trade mark protects the brand of a business by giving exclusive rights to use your brand within the area (class) in which you've registered it, stopping other competitors from using it for that purpose.
Both Peter and Deborah made an offer and after some negotiating, Imogen and Matt walked away with an investment from both Dragons, who each gave £25k for a 5% stake in the business.
A soup-er pitch

Bella Acland, founder of 'Soul Kitchen', pitched her healthy instant powdered soup brand to the Dragons. Inspired by her time in university relying on convenience foods, Bella set out to create something that wasn’t only convenient but comforting and nutritious.
Bella was asking the Dragons for £40k in return for 10% of the business.

It was clear that Bella had big aspirations for the business and had many ideas for future flavours and recipes. It got me thinking, how would she protect those flavours and ideas from being copied? The answer, trade secrets.
Trade secrets are not registered and they can help businesses protect recipes and processes so long as they are kept confidential.
If you do need to discuss or share your idea with someone else, you could consider a non-disclosure agreement (NDA). An NDA is a legal contract that sets out how confidential information is shared.
A single serving

While impressed with Bella and her pitch, the Dragons were not convinced it was an opportunity for them to invest in. After four "I'm outs", things were not looking great. Then Susie Ma stepped in, offering all the money in return for 15%. The offer was enthusiastically accepted by Bella.
This week’s episode had plenty of IP to think about. If you have an idea for a business, our free get IP rights step by step guidance can help you get started.

title: Shaping the future of occupational standards, by Tessa Griffiths and Sarah Maclean

content.content: It is vital that the skills system is in the best place possible to support growth and transform the lives and careers of people across the nation for years to come.
Occupational standards are at the heart of our technical education system, setting out the skills required to be competent in an occupation and helping to make sure training meets employers’ needs.

Our Skills for Work programme, led by Skills England’s board chair, Phil Smith, is considering how occupational standards and the training they underpin can better support growth, employers, places and young people.

This isn’t about individual standards – it’s about making sure the system is fit for the future. So, we are asking employers, training providers, sector bodies, unions, learners and regional leaders to share their views, based on their experience and expertise.
Purpose and scope
We are asking stakeholders to think about the following:
Why we are doing this

Defined by employers and other key stakeholders, occupational standards have played an important role in improving quality and matching training to employers’ needs. However, advances in technology and artificial intelligence, changing workforce demographics, evolving employer needs, and regional economic priorities are creating new demands on the skills system.
As the economy continues to evolve, it is important – and right – to check what’s working and what can be improved.
How to support
We will only succeed if our recommendations are informed by evidence, practical experience and a broad range of perspectives from across the skills system. We are asking stakeholders to support by:
This is your opportunity to make a positive difference, helping us build a system that works better than ever for employers, learners, and places.
Tessa Griffiths and Sarah Maclean
Joint Chief Executives, Skills England

title: Creating the conditions for transformation
authors: Jack Strachan, Senior Service Designer, CustomerFirst

content.content: CustomerFirst is a new unit within GDS learning what conditions help transformation teams succeed through a NewCo approach. Our first partnership is with the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency 's (DVLA) Drivers Medical service, which makes licensing decisions when a medical condition may affect someone's ability to drive, with consequences for people's independence, work and everyday life.

When we formed the joint DVLA and CustomerFirst team and began looking at the Drivers Medical service, we were also testing what conditions a NewCo approach requires: creating enough space around the team to pursue change, identify the constraints holding the service back and learn which freedoms actually matter.

In practice, that space is shaped by the organisation around the team because Drivers Medical cannot pause while we change it. Licensing decisions carry on being made every day, established processes still shape how they are made, and people carry years of knowledge about why the service works as it does. So, the way the team is set up, and the support around it, must respond to that context as much as to the methods the team uses.
We are still learning what those conditions need to be. Some of the choices we made at the beginning have already proved particularly important.
Create real capacity for the work
Before delivery began, senior stakeholders across DVLA and GDS agreed a commitment to a shared ambition for the transformation work and to protecting the conditions the team would need to pursue it.

Creating dedicated capacity was part of that agreement. Drivers Medical colleagues joining the joint team came out of their existing roles, with those roles backfilled, so they could work full-time alongside GDS colleagues.

Backfilling sounds like a resourcing detail, but it changes the relationship people have with the work. Transformation asks people to spend time understanding a problem, following evidence, testing ideas and making decisions together. That becomes much harder when the same people remain responsible for keeping their previous part of the organisation running.

Giving people real capacity has helped us build a joint team rather than two organisations collaborating around the edges of existing jobs. Relationships have developed through the work itself, and responsibility for where the work goes is shared. For us this has become one of the clearest NewCo conditions: enough protected capacity to organise around the service problem, rather than being repeatedly pulled back into responsibilities people already hold.
Bring organisational knowledge into the team
The people who know the existing organisation best are also some of the people best placed to help change it.

Drivers Medical colleagues understand why processes exist, how systems depend on one another, where previous attempts have struggled, and which apparent constraints may have more room to move than they first seem. That knowledge is difficult to reproduce through stakeholder interviews or occasional governance meetings because much of it sits in experience, relationships and practical judgement.

The value becomes clearer when the team starts trying things. An experiment may run into a technology constraint that has been treated as fixed for years. A different service model can surface questions about assurance, information governance or policy. Sometimes the team discovers that a constraint is protecting something important. Sometimes it finds an existing arrangement that can be approached differently.
Having that organisational knowledge inside the team helps us understand what we are dealing with before deciding what needs to happen next.
Work in the open, and know where authority sits

Working in the open is part of how we manage the boundary between decisions the team can make and those that need authority elsewhere. We share work and thinking early, so people around it can see what is changing and challenge it where useful. Visibility does not automatically create another approval step. Small tests give the team something concrete to decide against, reducing how much depends on assertion or hierarchy and keeping decisions close to the people doing the work.

When something does need authority elsewhere, the partnership gives us a route to senior sponsorship. We call this "air cover". Leaders have already committed to the conditions around the work, so escalation is about unblocking rather than re-stating the case. The judgement about when to use it matters. Escalating too quickly moves decisions away from the people closest to the work and turns senior sponsorship into part of the everyday operating model.

Each constraint we hit is useful information either way. It tells us where authority sits now, which decisions the team can make for itself, and where a wider organisational change may eventually be needed. For small experiments, the team works with assurance specialists to identify an approach that reflects the scale and nature of the risk. That keeps the team moving safely. It also shows us whether the existing assurance route fits this kind of work, and whether a constraint genuinely needs air cover or can be worked through within the team's own authority.
Learning what NewCo needs through delivery

We are still early in this work, and part of the NewCo hypothesis is that we should learn the operating model through delivery. Understanding why a constraint exists, what it is protecting and how fixed it really is can tell us as much as successfully removing it.

So far, three conditions have proved particularly important: creating real capacity for transformation work, bringing organisational knowledge into the team, and working in the open with clear routes for decision-making. These are conditions we would encourage other organisations to consider when setting up transformation work of their own.
As the work grows, we will keep testing where those boundaries need to sit and which of these conditions transfer to other transformation work across government.
If you are working through similar questions elsewhere in government, we would be interested to hear what you are learning too. You can contact the CustomerFirst team at customer.first@dsit.gov.uk.

title: Help shape our new contractual control service

content.content: As a user researcher at HM land Registry (HMLR), I work in a team whose goal is to make our services as easy-to-use as possible for customers. This means understanding any pain points in the user journey so we can do our best to reduce them.
The Provision of Information (Contractual Control) (Registered Land) Regulations 2026 (‘the Regulations’) legislation has been made and will come into force on 6 April 2027.

Information about certain land agreements such as options, conditional contracts and pre-emption rights where those agreements give a person the power to control how land is used or developed, is to be submitted digitally to HMLR through a regulated conveyancer.
We are currently developing a new service for conveyancers to record and submit this ‘contractual control’ information.
How you could help develop the service
We’re now approaching an important stage of development and would like to invite future users of the service to take part in our upcoming private beta phase this November.
If you are interested in taking part, please provide your details in the form linked to below and someone in the user research team will get back to you as soon as possible.
Who do we need to take part?
We’re looking for legal professionals who will be involved in recording and submitting contractual control information to HMLR when the service goes live.
Shaping the service to suit customers

So far this year we have engaged with around 31 legal firms and 48 individuals for user research, typically Professional Support Lawyers (PSLs), conveyancers, solicitors and legal assistants. We have also been engaging with legal professionals in other forums and working groups as well as other  stakeholders from the property industry, such as property developers, technology suppliers and local authorities.
Why take part?
This is an important opportunity for legal professionals to influence the service before its planned launch in April 2027.
During private beta, selected users will try the service before it launches. Their feedback will help us check that it works well and make improvements before it goes live.

The private beta will provide access to a fully functioning version of the service, (still subject to further changes), allowing you to help evaluate how effectively the new system will support your work and help you meet your obligations.
What do you need to do?
You can take part in whichever way works best for you. This may include:
•           remote sessions
•           submitting feedback via an online form
•           completing a short survey to share your experiences
•           face to face sessions
What previous participants have said

Earlier user research participants have commented: “It's so helpful for us to see the thinking and hopefully provide some useful feedback to you as well”, “It was quite illuminating” and “This is very helpful because it gives us an idea of how it's going to work out.”
How user research has shaped the service so far
User feedback has directly influenced the way we've designed the service to date.
Developing the service

While we want to create a user-centred service, we aren’t always able to incorporate everyone’s preferences, as we have to take things like legislation, technology, and the needs of people who will be using the data when it is published, into account.
Get involved
By taking part in the private beta testing, you can help us make the contractual control service as user-friendly as possible before it launches in April 2027.

We welcome your comments about this blog in the comments below. Please note that we are unable to discuss individual cases through the comments section and would request that all such queries be directed to our Contact Us web form where you will receive a response as soon as possible.

title: An update on how we use remote monitoring to support environmental land management agreements

content.content: Remote monitoring is one of the ways we check that funded environmental actions are achieving the expected results. It helps us to understand what is working well and identify where farmers and landowners would benefit from extra support.
Since our last blog in November 2025 on How RPA uses remote monitoring technology to monitor environmental land management (ELM) agreements, we’ve continued to develop and improve this work.
Improving our monitoring capabilities

Over the last year, we’ve continued to improve our remote monitoring capabilities by introducing additional monitoring markers and enhanced analysis techniques. These improvements help us understand how agreements are being delivered and assess how environmental actions are progressing over time.
Turning information into support

These new analysis techniques will help us identify where agreements are progressing well, where additional support may be needed, and where further information could help us understand what’s happening on the ground. This will improve the targeting of farm visits, help resolve issues earlier and help manage your agreements successfully.
Remote monitoring may show that:

When we identify a possible issue, we may contact you to ask for more information or evidence. This helps us understand whether the issue has been caused by management challenges, natural events outside your control, or a failure to meet agreement requirements.
If remote monitoring and our follow-up review show that the agreement requirements haven’t been met, we will reduce or recover the payment.
Change of circumstances
If you’re unable to meet the requirements of your agreement due to a change of circumstances, it’s important to let us know as soon as possible.
For more information, follow the instructions in the relevant guidance for your agreement year and scheme on GOV.UK.
Looking ahead

We’ll continue to develop our monitoring capabilities as new data and analysis techniques become available.  Remote monitoring will remain an important part of how we oversee ELM agreements to effectively manage taxpayers’ money. Our priority is to support successful agreement delivery and make sure public funding achieves the environmental outcomes it's intended to deliver.

title: Spectrum Technologies – to the moon and back

content.content: When you’re next sitting aboard a plane, consider the fact that there are many dozens or even hundreds of miles of electrical wiring on board, controlling the aircraft and feeding the technology around you. Fly-by-wire controls, avionics (electronic systems used on aircraft), reading lights, air conditioning and entertainment screens, as well as galley equipment and safety features - those miles of wiring interconnect to link everything back to the cockpit and cabin controls.

Now imagine you’re the electrical engineer working on that wiring – how do you distinguish between one wire and another, when some of it can be as narrow as 0.8mm in diameter with insulation about 3 times the diameter of a human hair?

Dr Peter Dickinson of Spectrum Technologies tells us how his business has commercialised innovative ways of marking identity codes on wires that are not only used across the world but are even circling us in space!
From solving a problem to creating a global standard

Spectrum Technologies was established in 1989 as a spin-out from British Aerospace (now BAE Systems). Spectrum’s founder member Dr Peter Dickinson was leading a programme in industrial laser technology at the company's research centre in Filton, Bristol.

At the time, the aerospace industry faced a growing challenge: aircraft wiring had traditionally been identified with alphanumeric codes using an ink-based impact marking process called hot stamping, a technique dating back to 1941. However, over the decades, aircraft electrical wiring interconnect systems (EWIS) grew in size and complexity, also growing in weight; the EWIS on a large jetliner now weighs in at several tonnes.

The ever-present need to minimise aircraft weight drove the requirement for lighter wiring, resulting in the insulation becoming much thinner and increasingly made from advanced non-stick materials, making it prone to damage. The old marking methods struggled to keep up and, in some cases, did damage the wiring itself.

Working with Airbus and other aerospace partners, Peter's team investigated alternative technologies and made a breakthrough using ultraviolet lasers. Unlike conventional laser processes that burn material away, the UV laser created a permanent mark by changing the colour of pigments within the insulation itself.
Recognising the commercial potential, British Aerospace tasked Peter with bringing the technology to market, leading to the creation of Spectrum Technologies.
What does this technology look like today?

Today, Spectrum Technologies’ ultraviolet laser wire-marking technology has become the global aerospace industry standard. Spectrum designs and manufactures the highly specialised laser-based systems used to mark, identify, strip and process wire and cable assemblies. Its headquarters in Bridgend is supported by teams across the world, doing business in Europe, North America, Asia, the Middle East, Africa, South America and Australia.

The company's systems are used by virtually every major aerospace manufacturer, including Boeing, Airbus, Lockheed Martin, SpaceX and BAE Systems. The technology may be unseen by airline passengers, but it plays a critical role in aviation. Individual wires must be uniquely identified to enable efficient manufacture, maintenance and repair throughout the aircraft's lifetime.
Some 'plane' facts
Spectrum’s technology is also used on military platforms, satellites, medical devices, consumer electronics and space missions.

“Our laser wire marking is used primarily for aerospace and some rail and defence electrical wiring interconnection systems (EWIS ) applications, whereas our laser wire stripping is used foremost in the electronics and medical sectors”, Peter told us.
Spectrum in space - technology used on Moon and Mars missions and beyond
Spectrum equipment has been used to produce wiring for:
As Peter puts it: "Pretty much anything flying today that's been built in the last 20-30 years will have wiring identified using the technology we developed."
How has IP helped commercialise the technology?

Intellectual property (IP) protection has been central to Spectrum's commercial success. Spectrum has worked with IP specialists, patent attorneys Wynne-Jones IP since the early 1990s and values their guidance in assessing patentability, drafting applications and developing international filing strategies. Peter believes patents were particularly valuable in the company's formative years:

Over the years, Spectrum has successfully protected its technology and, in one case, negotiated a licence agreement after identifying a competitor using patented technology in the UK market. Peter is quick to point out that obtaining effective patent protection requires careful preparation, however.

He is keen to stress the importance of identifying the core innovation, undertaking thorough prior-art searches and working with experienced patent attorneys. Peter’s message to innovators is simple:
What's next for Spectrum Technologies?

The company is expanding its automation capabilities, developing new systems and working on laser marking solutions for highly specialised medical applications, surgical instruments and medical devices.So, where can Spectrum possibly go after becoming the global aerospace standard and circling space? With a smile, Peter offers his answer:
“First global domination, then the solar system, and after that, perhaps the galaxy!”
For a South Wales business whose technology is already helping power some of humanity's most ambitious engineering achievements, it may not be quite as fanciful as it sounds.

title: Beyond the clinics: What a week at the VMD taught me about the regulation of medicines

content.content: In May 2026, a cohort of veterinary students visited the Veterinary Medicines Directorate (VMD) as part of their Extramural Studies placement. One of the students, Victoria, shared her experience of the placement.

As veterinary students, our training is understandably centred on the diagnosis and treatment of the animals in front of us. It is easy to forget that behind every drug we will prescribe as vets is a system working to make sure it is safe and effective. A placement at the VMD offered a valuable reminder that the profession's impact extends well beyond the consulting room and gave us a glimpse into a side of veterinary medicine most students rarely think about.
Prescribing through a regulatory lens

The week opened with an overview of the VMD's role, both nationally and internationally, before moving into sessions on antimicrobial and anthelmintic resistance. We all know that responsible prescribing matters, but seeing the issue from a regulatory perspective helped put our future role as veterinary surgeons into a wider context. It provided a reminder that prescribing decisions made in a consultation ripple outward into public health and food security, and that responsible use of antimicrobials and antiparasitics is as much a regulatory concern as a clinical one. Participating in discussions on policy making made the scale of the issue feel far more tangible than it ever had in a lecture theatre.
Demystifying veterinary medicines regulations

From there, sessions on the enforcement of medicines regulations, authorisation of veterinary medicines, and inspections provided real insight into how veterinary medicines are assessed and monitored, before and after they reach the market. It was interesting to see just how many checks a product goes through before it reaches a clinic’s pharmacy, and how that scrutiny does not stop once it has been authorised. Further sessions focused on biologicals and novel therapies, followed by a bioequivalence and generics workshop which highlighted just how complex the pathway from product development to authorisation really is. Discussions on quality assurance, legislation, and environmental safety underlined the breadth of expertise needed to keep the whole system running.
Life beyond clinical practice

Perhaps the biggest surprise of the week was discovering the range of veterinary careers that exist outside clinical practice. Careers discussions throughout the placement gave us insight into varied roles in regulation, policy, legislation, research, and public health. A useful reminder that a veterinary degree can lead in many directions, and that veterinary knowledge is valuable even when you're not working directly with animals every day.

By the end of the week, I had a completely new appreciation for the medicines I will be prescribing every day, and a much better sense of the machinery that keeps them safe. This is the kind of placement that does not show up in a typical EMS advert, but honestly, more of us should know it exists.
Victoria Young

title: Testing the new Driver Services Platform: our trial in Durham

content.content: We’re developing the Driver Services Platform (DSP) to modernise how we manage driving test bookings.

Earlier this summer we ran a small-scale trial at Durham Driving Test Centre (DTC) to test how key parts of the system work in a live environment. Now the trial is complete we can share more details about what we were testing, how it went and the next steps in the journey to a new booking service.
A quick recap: why are we making a new booking system?
If you’ve not read our previous blog posts you might be wondering what the new system is. You can find the previous blog post here.
DSP will replace the current booking system. The new system will make the process of booking a practical driving test much more user focused.
Initially we are focusing on car tests, but will later roll out to the other areas, such as instructor, motorcycle and vocational tests.
Now, back to the trial.
Taking small steps
Smaller scale trials allow us to test each part of the system before rolling it out further. For this trial we wanted to test 4 key parts:

To do this properly, we needed to try the system out with real learners going through the process of booking and taking their test. We booked a small sample of 14 learners into DSP over 2 testing days at Durham DTC.
We chose Durham as it’s fairly average in terms of its size, staffing levels and test throughput.

During the trial we wanted to check that the functionality built into the system, so far, worked as intended. That meant a lot of manual work in the background to get things ready. This included setting up test centres and examiners, building examiner shift patterns, creating customer profiles, allocating test dates and times, taking payments and making sure the results emails work once the test has finished.
It’s not as simple as it might first seem.
Working with local ADIs

Before testing could begin, we needed the support of local approved driving instructors (ADIs). So, we held an event with the local driving test centre manager to introduce the trial to ADIs in the area, generate interest and invite them to put their pupils forward.
Around 35 people attended and 11 ADIs signed up on the day, giving us a pool of 36 learners who were test ready and flexible on timing.
What we did
We worked with local ADIs to volunteer their pupils who would be ready to take their test around June/July. For this initial trial, we were looking for learner drivers taking a standard car test.

As we are still in the very early stages of testing, the ability to book tests with additional requirements such as a double slot, with a Welsh speaking examiner, or in an adapted vehicle will come in later phases.

We filled all the test slots in time for our 2 main testing days on 23 and 30 July. Throughout this process, our small transition team of 3 managed the process manually: contacting ADIs and learners by phone within limited hours, collecting customer data and recording everything securely.
Was it a success?
We are very pleased with the outcome.
As strange as it sounds the intention was for learner drivers to not notice any difference when taking the test, just the process to book it.

From our perspective, the tests were in the system and on the examiner's tablet and were ready for when the tests were due to start. The results of the test were shared with DVLA and full licences, when the test was successful, were sent quickly.
Of course, not everything ran smoothly, but this is the point of the trial. Running into any  issues in a smaller controlled environment allowed them to be fixed and a solution found for next time.
The next major step for the new system is to get the same level of success from a trial, but with less manual input.
Next steps

This trial was a valuable and encouraging first step, but it's important to be clear that DSP is still very much a work in progress and there is more testing and development ahead before it's ready for wider use.
In the short term, we've already made improvements based on what we learned. The next big step is to improve the new system to be able to do more steps on its own such as payments and choosing dates.

We want to be upfront that getting DSP right will take time. This won't happen overnight and we'd rather take the time needed to test thoroughly and build confidence in the system than move faster and risk getting it wrong. Each trial gives us more confidence, and more evidence, to build on before we scale up further.
We'll continue to share updates as DSP development progresses.

title: Nature Restoration Fund: turning national ambition into practical action in Norfolk

content.content: The launch of the first Environmental Delivery Plan consultation by Natural England is about more than a new process. It is the first opportunity to test, in a real place and with the people who know it best, a new approach to delivering the homes we need while helping nature recover.

The government is reforming the planning system to support the delivery of new homes and critical infrastructure, whilst improving outcomes for the environment, and the Nature Restoration Fund is a key part of that effort.
From national reform to local delivery

The Nature Restoration Fund (NRF) was established through the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 to provide a quicker and simpler way for developers to meet their responsibilities regarding protected sites and species, while enabling more impactful conservation action to be delivered.

Developers generally have to assess and mitigate environmental impacts project-by-project. That can at times create complexity and uncertainty for developers, and result in specific interventions that address an individual development’s impact without necessarily contributing to wider nature recovery.

The NRF offers an alternative. Through ‘Environmental Delivery Plans’, Natural England will assess specified impacts from development in an area, identify a package of conservation measures and set a levy that developers can choose to pay if they opt in, discharging their obligations with regard to protected habitats and species. Contributions from different developments can then be pooled, allowing Natural England and its partners to deliver coordinated action that delivers an overall improvement for nature.
Why Norfolk, and why now?

The first draft Environmental Delivery Plan focuses on addressing the impact of nutrient pollution affecting protected sites in Norfolk. These are internationally important landscapes, supporting rare habitats, distinctive wildlife and highly sensitive ecosystems. They are also part of local communities that need more homes.

The plan has capacity to enable over 15,000 new houses. Once developers have paid into the NRF, it will fund a range of impactful conservation measures that will make a real difference on the ground. This includes river and wetland restoration, the creation of freshwater habitats and wetland habitat management, Together, these measures will strengthen the resilience of Norfolk’s rivers, wetlands and protected habitats for the long term.
Environmental Delivery Plan consultation

In developing the plan, we have worked closely with local stakeholders to ensure that it reflects local needs and priorities. Natural England is now launching a consultation to gather further input. In particular, we want them to hear from people who live and work in Norfolk and further understand its places, pressures and opportunities.

This consultation is an opportunity to test the evidence and scrutinise the proposed conservation measures and delivery arrangements before the plan is finalised. It will also provide valuable lessons for the wider implementation of the Nature Restoration Fund.
Help us get it right
This first consultation marks the point at which national reform begins to take shape on the ground.
The Environmental Delivery Plan is designed to provide greater certainty for communities, developers and local authorities, and deliver meaningful, lasting recovery for nature.

That is why we’re encouraging local communities, developers, environmental organisations, nature-market suppliers, land managers and local planning authorities to examine the proposals and share their views.

By bringing together national reform, local knowledge and practical experience, we can help build an approach that delivers for Norfolk and provides a strong foundation for the Nature Restoration Fund across England.

title: England's salmon stocks: what the latest data tells us

content.content: Atlantic salmon are a remarkable and iconic species. Hatching in rivers across Northern Europe, they migrate thousands of miles across the North Atlantic to feed and grow before returning to those same rivers to spawn.

Every year, the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science, the Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales report on the state of our salmon stock levels, to help determine actions needed to protect this species. This annual assessment provides key insights into the health of salmon populations in England's principal salmon rivers, giving an important evidence base for understanding population trends, identifying rivers most at risk and helping target recovery activity where it can have the greatest impact.

The latest assessment, based on data from 2025 shows that Atlantic salmon stocks remain at critically low levels, with 40 of England's 42 principal salmon rivers projected to be classified as either "at risk" or "probably at risk" in 2030. This means 95% of our salmon rivers are at risk of having a salmon population below the level required for a long term sustainable population. This is not an isolated trend. Most salmon stocks across other UK  jurisdictions and the wider North Atlantic are facing similar patterns.
Why are salmon declining?

There is no single reason for the decline in salmon populations.  This problem is not unique to England and is observable across the North Atlantic. Much of the cause lies at sea and beyond the control of any single country.

Salmon face multiple pressures throughout their lives in rivers and in the sea, with freshwater habitats affected by pollution, migration barriers on rivers and water scarcity and marine habitats impacted by factors such as aquaculture and bycatch. Climate change is intensifying these impacts.
The decline seen today is the result of many of these pressures interacting over time, rather than any single cause.
Why are salmon important?
Atlantic salmon are one of England's most iconic fish species and an important indicator of environmental health.
Because they depend on healthy rivers, estuaries and seas throughout their lives, the health of salmon populations can tell us a great deal about the condition of the wider environment.
Efforts to improve conditions for salmon can also benefit many other species and help create healthier rivers for people and wildlife.
Is this just happening in England?

No. Salmon populations are facing challenges across much of the North Atlantic. Similar declines are being reported in other parts of the UK and internationally.  This highlights the scale and complexity of the challenge facing the species.
What is being done to help salmon recover?

Action to improve conditions for salmon recovery includes improving river flows, restoring habitats, improving fish passage, tackling pollution, supporting catchment partnerships, fisheries enforcement activity and improving scientific understanding of the pressures affecting salmon populations.
Recovery will require sustained action from government, regulators, water companies, environmental organisations, anglers, land managers and local communities.
Why is recovery taking so long?
Salmon have a complex lifecycle. Young salmon can spend up to three years in rivers before migrating to sea, where they may spend one or two years before returning to spawn.
This means it can take several years before improvements in habitat, river health or migration routes are reflected in salmon population numbers.
Recovery is therefore a long-term effort, requiring sustained action over many years.
Can salmon populations in England recover?
Yes. While they remain under significant pressure, recovery is possible when conditions improve.
There are examples from across England where action to improve water quality, restore habitat and reconnect rivers has helped create opportunities for salmon populations to recover.
Recovery takes time, but practical action can help create the conditions salmon need to thrive.
What is the Environment Agency’s role in helping salmon recover?
The Environment Agency has a statutory duty to maintain, improve and develop salmon populations and fisheries in England.

Salmon recovery requires coordinated action across multiple sectors  by a range of organisations, including government, international partners, water companies, farmers, local authorities, anglers and fishing communities and NGOs.

We are therefore active in working with partners to address the pressures affecting salmon in both freshwater and marine environments.  One example of this partnership work is the Great Yorkshire Rivers partnership.

EA is also an active member of the North Atlantic Salmon Conservation Organisation (NASCO). To deal with the impacts of low river flows, pollution and physical barriers that block access to spawning habitat Defra and the Environment Agency have launched a long-term recovery programme through the NASCO, uniting government, regulators, water companies and catchment partnerships to tackle these three pressures together. Running from 2026 to 2032, the programme is improving river flows in priority catchments, cracking down on pollution through increased inspections and wastewater oversight, and restoring habitats by removing barriers, improving fish passage and planting trees to keep rivers cool and resilient.

The EA will restore 2,282 hectares of peatland and improve water flow below reservoirs, so rivers have enough water even during dry spells. It will also closely monitor water companies and other users to ensure they are not taking more water than rivers can sustain.

Alongside this, the EA will carry out more inspections of farms and wastewater treatment works, and fund over 800 projects to cut pollution from wastewater. We will also clear or improve 105 barriers that block salmon from reaching their spawning grounds, restore natural river habitat at 252 sites, and plant 648 hectares of trees along riverbanks to keep the water cool and clean.

title: Teacher pay: everything you need to know about the latest multi- year pay award

content.content: Here’s everything you need to know about teacher pay.

The School Teachers' Review Body (STRB) is an independent group that makes recommendations on the pay of teachers and leaders in maintained schools in England and reports to the Secretary of State for Education and the Prime Minister.

Each year the STRB recommends a pay award based on different factors including the economy, school workforce data and evidence from organisations including the DfE, employers, and unions.https://educationhub.blog.gov.uk/category/trade-unions/
The government then considers the recommendations in depth and makes a decision on what pay award teachers receive.
In order to give schools and teachers more certainty over pay and their budgets, the Education Secretary asked the STRB’s to make recommendations for a multi-year pay award for the next two years.
Are teachers getting a pay rise?

The STRB recommended that from September 2026, teachers and leaders will receive a pay award of 3.5%, followed by a further 3% increase from September 2027. These recommendations have been accepted in full, reflecting the crucial role teachers play in breaking the link between background and success for pupils.

This means school teachers will see an increase in their pay of 17% since this government took power - equating to almost £7,900 over four years - with the average school teacher salary rising to over £52,800 from September 2026 and over £54,400 from September 2027.
You can calculate how your salary could change following pay award here.
Will teachers at all schools receive the pay award?
The pay award applies to maintained schools currently, but most academies also choose to follow the statutory pay arrangements in practice.

Through the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, the government will ensure all teachers in academies as well as maintained schools can rely on a core pay offer and will require academies to have regard to the School Teachers Pay and Conditions Document, expected to be implemented by September 2027.
We will continue to increase flexibilities into the national pay and conditions framework so that all schools can innovate to attract and retain brilliant teachers.
Is the pay award fully funded?

This multi-year pay deal award is backed by a significant additional investment of £700 million in 2026-27 and £1.1 billion in 27-28, meaning a total of £1.8 billion more for schools over the next two years, on top of the funding increases which the government has already provided through the 2025 Spending Review.

Recent valuations to the Local Government Pension Scheme will see a 4.9ppt reduction in employer contribution rates and deliver significant savings on schools’ pay bill for support staff. We can confirm this reduction in costs will not be clawed back and as such, we are confident that schools will be able to cover the costs of the teacher pay award, at a national level.
As with the rest of the public sector, schools will continue to maximise value from their budgets.
How can schools maximise and get better value from their budgets?
We know this is not an easy task. Schools are already working hard to manage pressures on budgets.  That’s why we are providing support through the Maximising Value for Pupils programme.

Through the programme we are using the collective weight of the entire school system to help every school get more from every pound, so that money reaches the classroom where it matters most. This includes help to cut the cost on things like energy and recruitment, as well as providing better banking solutions.
For example:
When will teachers receive their pay rise?

The pay award now goes through a 12 week period of consultation with unions and employers’ organisations. The school teachers' pay conditions (STPCD) which sets out teachers pay and conditions, will then be published in mid-October for schools to implement. The pay award will be back-dated to 1st September.
Will school support staff get a pay rise?

The teacher pay award only applies to school teachers, but the additional funding schools will receive also takes into account the current pay offer for support staff, which is currently under negotiation.

Unlike teachers, most school support staff are currently employed on the pay and conditions of the National Joint Council (NJC) for Local Government Services. The NJC is a negotiating body made up of representatives from trade unions and local government employers.  NJC employees have been offered a 3.3% pay increase from 1 April 2026, which remains subject to agreement through the NJC collective bargaining process.

The School Support Staff Negotiating Body (SSSNB) is expected to be established from this autumn to give support staff like teaching assistants, caretakers and cleaners a stronger voice. The body will bring together employer and employee representatives to negotiate pay, terms and conditions, and to advise on training and career progression.
Will further education teachers get a pay rise?

The Department for Education does not set further education pay. However, we are providing £485 million in additional funding over two years to support colleges and other further education providers to address immediate staffing pressures, boosting opportunity for learners and driving skills for growth.
What else are you doing to ensure teaching is an attractive profession?
We are continuing to work alongside schools and colleges to re-establish teaching as the attractive, expert profession it should be.

This includes investing hundreds of millions of pounds to offer tax free financial incentives and professional development to attract and keep brilliant teachers alongside targeted action to improve teachers’ wellbeing.

This is working with the latest figures showing the government is on track to meet its manifesto pledge to recruit and retain an additional 6,500 expert teachers with 4,654 more secondary school, special school and college teachers.

We have made strong progress on teacher recruitment and retention with one of the lowest rates of schoolteachers leaving in the history of the school workforce census – at 2,100 fewer teachers than last year, and there has been a 13% rise in people training to teach, with the STEM recruitment target surpassed for the first time since it was introduced.
How are you improving working conditions for school teachers?

We are also making changes to the School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document. This includes enabling maintained schools to offer modest non-consolidated recognition payments to staff, as academies already do, so they too can offer recognition schemes to reward their staff; increasing flexibility on INSET days so that schools can structure training in the way which works best for staff and pupils, and clarifying the protections for leaders' working time, including the right to uninterrupted breaks and expectations that weekends and, public holiday should ordinarily be preserved as non-working time.

title: Protecting the Thames Basin Heaths: evidence from 15 years of the SAMM Project

content.content: By Zoe Shorter, Project Manager for the SAMM Team, Thames Solent Area Team

This blog explains the findings of an independent evaluation of the 15-year Thames Basin Heaths SAMM Project. Evidence suggests the project is successfully mitigating recreational pressure on protected heathlands, with stable or increasing bird populations despite housing growth, and the report has identified wardening, education and partnership work as key strengths.
Spanning across Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire, the Thames Basin Heaths is a stunning collection of lowland heathland of international importance.

The landscape is home to an incredible range of flora and fauna, including every species of native reptile, rare Silver-studded Blue and Grayling butterflies, a dazzling array of dragonflies, and rare birds including the Nightjar, Dartford Warbler and Woodlark.

For the last 15 years, the Thames Basin Heaths Strategic Access Management and Monitoring (SAMM) Project has worked to reduce recreational pressure on internationally important heathland habitats while helping local communities continue to enjoy them.
This September, we are pleased to share the findings of an independent evaluation of the project.
Building better places for people and nature

The Thames Basin Heaths Partnership brings together local authorities, Natural England, conservation organisations, land managers and other partners to protect the Thames Basin Heaths Special Protection Area, while supporting sustainable development across Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire.

At the heart of the partnership is a simple ambition: that everyone living within Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire, values the Thames Basin Heaths, feels a sense of responsibility towards them and is motivated to help protect them.
As part of this partnership, the SAMM team works towards this through monitoring, education and engagement activities that promote three core messages:
Alongside SAMM, the partnership offer alternative places to walk and enjoy nature, reducing pressure on protected heathlands and helping balance nature conservation with development.

At Natural England, we are committed to building better places where nature and communities can coexist. We believe that nature and development go hand in hand, and that we should harness the power of nature as we face a changing climate.
The work done by the SAMM team directly supports these aims.
Asking the important question: how do we know we’re being effective?
Although reviewing and monitoring were built into the strategic solution from the outset, a formal evaluation of the SAMM Project had never been undertaken.

Discussions with Natural England colleagues and other projects that help reduce the environmental impacts of new development, at the annual National Mitigation Meet Ups, revealed a shared challenge: demonstrating the impact of behaviour change and preventative conservation work.
In 2024, funding was secured to commission an independent evaluation of the SAMM Project, gathering evidence, identifying improvements and helping to inform future delivery of the project.
The review focused on 4 key questions:
Evaluation outcomes
We were delighted to find the evaluation showed the project is delivering on its core aims.

The headline finding though was that despite significant housing growth and increased visitor numbers across the area, protected bird populations have remained stable and in some cases  increased; indicating that the project has successfully mitigated recreational impacts on the Thames Basin Heaths.

The report identifies our wardening, education and partnership work as key strengths of the project. These activities are at the heart of what we do, helping people enjoy the heathlands while understanding how to protect them. Through guided walks, public events, school visits and community outreach, we connect thousands of people with these special places every year.

The evaluation found that wardens are particularly effective at building trust with visitors through regular conversations, while the education programme has grown significantly in recent years. Together, these activities help build awareness, encourage responsible behaviour and inspire people to care for the Thames Basin Heaths.
Turning evidence into action

So far, we've been able to take the findings of this report and begin making some suggested improvements, including expanding our education capacity to meet the demand and making greater use of social media and other digital channels to reach new audiences.
We're also pleased to see the evaluation already generating interest beyond the partnership, with findings being shared and discussed by other teams working in mitigation and nature conservation.
We look forward to 15 more years of fantastic work protecting the Thames Basin Heaths.
Find out more
If you'd like to learn more, we encourage you to:
And if you're visiting your local heathland, please remember our three simple messages: stay on the path, be wildfire aware and help protect these special places for future generations.
You can also make a direct contribution by exploring our volunteering opportunities and getting involved in protecting the Thames Basin Heaths.
Finally, thank you to everyone who contributed to this work, including our partners, Joint Strategic Partnership Board members, Natural England colleagues, stakeholders and the wider SAMM team.
Together, we're building the evidence, partnerships and confidence needed to protect these internationally important heathlands while supporting thriving communities around them.

title: Bluetongue: how the Animal Health and Welfare Pathway can support farmers
categories: Payments to support animal health and welfare

content.content: Bluetongue virus is a notifiable disease that affects sheep, cattle, deer, goats and camelids - alpacas and llamas. It is mainly spread by midges but can also pass through infected semen, embryos or oocytes, or from a mother to her unborn offspring.
This summer’s hot weather has been ideal conditions for midges and helped the virus spread quicker.
Bluetongue cases are increasing across Great Britain. The disease is most prevalent in the Southwest, West Midlands, Northwest of England and in parts of Wales.

All of England is in a bluetongue Restricted Zone. Provided animals are not showing clinical signs, keepers can move animals within England without a specific bluetongue licence or pre-movement testing. Separate restricted zones are in place in Wales and southwest Scotland where there are also bluetongue outbreaks.

With cases rising quickly, testing demand has increased significantly. Defra introduced new reporting measures last week to speed up diagnosis, reduce waiting times and help farmers act sooner to protect their livestock.
In this post, we look at the new measures, steps livestock keepers can take to protect animals and upcoming webinars for more information.
New reporting measures in England for bluetongue
We know this is a difficult time for animal keepers dealing with Bluetongue. Defra and the Animal & Plant Health Agency (APHA) are working with farmers and vets to manage the outbreak.
In England, private vets can now diagnose clear cases of bluetongue after examining affected animals.

The new process makes it quicker and easier to confirm clear cases of bluetongue based on clinical signs. Private vets will contact the APHA to formally confirm diagnosis, instead of taking blood samples for testing.
This means straightforward cases do not need to wait for laboratory results, helping farmers get answers sooner and act quickly to protect their livestock.

The new changes don’t mean a reduction in disease controls. The usual safeguards remain in place. Where a vet cannot rule out suspicion of notifiable disease, including foot and mouth, the usual reporting and laboratory testing arrangements will continue.

These new changes reflect the current outbreak in England, where bluetongue is now widespread and well understood. These measures to help tackle bluetongue sit alongside wider disease surveillance and APHA support.
Details on how to spot and report bluetongue can be found on GOV.UK.
Support and actions for farmers
Sheep and cattle farmers in England can apply for a government-funded vet visit through the Animal Health and Welfare Pathway. The online application takes less than two minutes.
During the visit, vets can check animals for signs of disease, advise on bluetongue risks and suggest ways to reduce them.
Vaccination is the best way to help protect livestock from bluetongue. It is not too late this season, so farmers should speak to their vet and order vaccines as soon as possible.
Government is working with manufacturers to increase vaccine supply. Farmers should start planning for vaccination next year as the virus is likely to overwinter.
Livestock keepers can help reduce the spread of bluetongue by taking a few practical steps:
If you suspect bluetongue or another notifiable disease, contact your vet promptly. You can find more information and guidance on bluetongue on GOV.UK.

title: Have Your Say: Shape the Future of Working in Adult Social Care

content.content: Oonagh Smyth CBE is Chief Executive Officer of  Skills for Care, the strategic workforce planning and development body for adult social care in England. Here, she addresses the adult social care workforce on the importance of taking part in the Adult Social Care Workforce Survey.

This is an important time for adult social care. The Prime Minister has been clear about his commitment to supporting the workforce: the government is taking forward the Fair Pay Agreement and looking at the wider changes needed to make social care an attractive and rewarding career, including progression opportunities, training and better support for staff.
People working in adult social care know the job better than anyone. You know what makes it rewarding, what makes it difficult and what would make your working life better.
That is why we want to hear from you.

The Adult Social Care Workforce Survey is an opportunity to share your experiences directly with the Government. The survey is open to anyone who works in a care-related role in adult social care in England. Whether you work in a residential or domiciliary setting – as a care worker, a personal assistant, a manager, or a regulated professional (e.g. nurse, occupational therapist) - your voice matters.
Your experience can help shape what comes next

To make good decisions for tomorrow’s social care workforce, we need strong evidence about the realities of working in the sector today. The survey is your opportunity to help the Department of Health and Social Care understand what is working well, where the pressures are and what needs to improve.
Your voice will inform what the government does next to support the workforce.
Tell us what working in adult social care is really like
There are no right or wrong answers. We want your honest experience, including the positive parts of your work and the challenges you face.
The survey asks about the issues that can affect your day-to-day working life, including:

You may also have heard about Baroness Casey’s Big Conversation on Care. The two exercises complement each other but have different purposes. The Big Conversation invites everyone in England to discuss the bigger questions about the future of adult social care, whereas this survey focuses on the experience of working in care in detail. Each will provide different evidence to inform the future of adult social care.
Why your response matters

The more people who take part, the stronger and more representative the evidence will be. Each response adds to our understanding of working life across adult social care and helps show where change and support are most needed.
Do not assume somebody else will have the same experience or raise the same issues. Your perspective is unique, and without it, part of the picture will be missing.
Your responses will be kept confidential and reported alongside those of other participants. You will not be identified in the survey findings.
Take part in the survey
If you work in adult social care in England, please add your voice:
Take part in the Adult Social Care Workforce Survey – it takes just 20 minutes.
If you are a manager or employer, please encourage everyone in your organisation to participate and support them to complete the survey during working hours.
The future of adult social care should not be shaped without the people who work in it. Make sure your experience is part of the conversation.

title: How we made it easier for millions of users to sign into government services

content.content: This month, the Government Digital Service (GDS) made it faster, easier and more secure to sign into government services.

23 million people are already using GOV.UK One Login to sign in to over 250 UK government services. Now those users can use a passkey to sign in. This will be the same familiar way they unlock their device, for example with their face, fingerprint or passcode. Users will no longer need to remember a password or enter a security code (also known as ‘multi-factor authentication’) to sign in.

Passkeys are recommended by the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) for use wherever possible. They are more secure than passwords and less vulnerable to phishing and other cybersecurity attacks.

In the first month since we rolled out passkeys for GOV.UK One Login, we have already seen 300,000 (almost 10%) of our users are using them. In the years to come, we expect passkeys to save millions a year for the UK taxpayer by cutting the cost of text message-based authentication.
Introducing passkeys is just one of the ways we are making sure that digital public services are simple, trusted, secure and effective.
This is the biggest change we have made to the sign-in experience of GOV.UK One Login since it launched in 2021.
Putting the user first
The principle of designing for everyone is central to our work at GDS. We put this at the heart of our product development process.
To understand user perception and concerns about passkeys, we started by surveying over 2,500 people. We gathered evidence from user research, data analytics and industry insights.

We know that the public are increasingly using biometrics in many parts of their online lives, from banking to online shopping. This change helps create a more familiar sign-in experience and reflects wider changes in how people interact online.

We found that users struggle to remember passwords, so they reuse them and write them down. We also know that entering a security code is hard for many users, especially those with cognitive barriers and low digital confidence, and people who use assistive technology.
Our product strategy at GDS is to focus on meeting the needs of our users. We expect passkeys to cut the time it takes to sign in to GOV.UK One Login by more than half.
Everyone has needs

We know that for GOV.UK One Login users, authentication is not their end goal. It is a step users need to get through to completing a task, such as renewing their driving licence. Signing in should not be an obstacle for users. Passkeys can help remove the need for them to need to think about this step.

We applied this user-led approach to our wider product delivery too. Our design team set out to design our new passkeys user journeys collaboratively, by considering the needs of our technical architects, product managers, software developers, security experts and senior managers. We worked together to build the best possible user experience.

During our design process we ran workshops with developers to ensure design feasibility. They then checked back with designers to ensure usability. We also consulted security, fraud, and privacy experts to meet GOV.UK One Login’s high service quality standards. Our product manager steered our priorities by relentlessly asking "what is the user need?".
Passkeys have been a real collaboration for our team.
User research is a team sport

A design challenge was explaining passkeys in simple terms that our users will understand. This is especially challenging as how users will sign in can be different depending on their device. A passkey could be a fingerprint for one user, or a screen lock PIN for another. If users do not understand what they need to do, this can stop them from setting up a passkey.

Concerns about biometric data privacy can make users hesitate or worry. In reality, the user’s passkey is private. It is securely stored in their password manager. We had to explain technical concepts in clear, accessible language.

So, we tested our journeys with real users, including those with low digital confidence. In the past year we have run three rounds of user research and iterated our designs after each round. We learnt that users did not need to understand how passkeys work to be able to use them with ease. We worked closely with accessibility experts to design and test our journeys to make sure they work for all users, including those who use assistive technology.

We involved our entire product team, including developers, delivery managers, and product managers. They joined planning workshops, took notes during research sessions, and helped to interpret our findings. This helped our team build empathy for our users and gives us confidence that they will understand our service journeys.
Nudging users - learning from the industry

To ease the cognitive burden for users, we reviewed passkeys journeys across all major tech platforms and online services. This helped us to make sure we were giving users familiar, established content patterns.
Using guidelines from authentication industry experts the FIDO Alliance, we prompted users to set up a passkey during relevant moments in their journey, such as when they sign in.

NHS Login had already introduced passkeys. They shared their user-experience design insights with us about what they had learned. We also met with the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to learn from their work and share our designs.
Passkeys are live but we are not finished

To help us test passkeys safely with real users, our developers built a way for us to release our designs gradually to a small percentage of users. This meant we could check for any problems before we rolled them out to everyone.
We will continuously improve our passkeys user experience based on user insights, and by monitoring adoption rates - such as how many users reject passkeys in favour of their familiar sign in method.

It is going to take time for everyone in the UK to adopt passkeys. We know that not all of our users will be ready to use them straight away. But this development is a major step in the right direction for a user experience that is safer, easier and more secure for years to come.

title: Building hydrographic capability in St Helena

content.content: Safe navigation relies on accurate hydrographic data, and collecting that data requires skilled surveyors, specialist equipment, and local expertise. For a remote island such as St Helena, located in the South Atlantic, having this capability locally is particularly important.

Through its longstanding partnership with St Helena Government, the UKHO has provided loaned survey equipment and practical training to local teams. This is helping St Helena to collect vital seabed mapping data and support the safe and secure supply of goods to the island community.
Why is supporting hydrographic capacity building important?

Hydrography is the science that measures and describes the physical features of the seabed. Accurate hydrographic data underpins safe navigation, environmental management, and sustainable use of the marine environment. However, collecting and maintaining that data requires specialist equipment, technical expertise, and the ability to undertake surveys on an ongoing basis.

For island nations such as St Helena, developing local hydrographic capability ensures the mariners on board vessels approaching the remote island have access to fit-for-purpose information and helps to maintain the safe and secure supply of essential food and goods for its community.

Hydrographic data also enables coastal states like St Helena to gain further insights into the marine environment. Seabed mapping data provides marine scientists with information on marine habitats, as well as supporting decision-making for environmental protection and management.

As a world leader in hydrography, the UKHO shares its expertise with the global hydrographic community and actively supports the UK Overseas Territories and other partners, to develop their hydrographic capabilities.  In St Helena, the UKHO has provided access to specialist expertise, training, and state-of-the-art hydrographic survey equipment to undertake essential surveys within its port. By empowering local teams to collect, process, and manage hydrographic data themselves, the UKHO supports long-term resilience while improving the information used to update official navigational products.
Building capability through practical training

The capacity development has formed part of a longstanding partnership between the UKHO and St Helena Government, which aims to strengthen local hydrographic capability and support the collection of high-quality seabed mapping data around the island.

Following an introduction to hydrographic surveying and the systems involved, UKHO hydrographic experts spent two weeks working alongside marine stakeholders in St Helena. They shared practical surveying techniques and provided hands-on training in the use of the UKHO’s loaned survey equipment. Staff from St Helena’s Geographical Information Systems, Marine and Meteorological departments developed the skills needed to collect, process and manage seabed mapping data independently.
Using new technology in St Helena

Through its Hydrographic survey Equipment Loan Pool (HELP), the UKHO provided access to an uncrewed surface vessel (USV) equipped with an advanced multibeam echosounder.  The all-in-one survey platform enabled the team to begin surveying the island's waters immediately.  UKHO hydrographic experts then worked alongside local stakeholders, providing hands-on training and building the skills and confidence needed to operate the system safely in shallow and coastal waters around St Helena.

As well as supporting hydrographic surveys, USVs can be used in a range of operational situations, including search and rescue activities and environmental monitoring. This makes them a flexible tool for St Helena's marine community, while producing fewer emissions than traditional survey vessels.

The initial training focused on using the USV to monitor the port environment and support the safe arrival of supply vessels. In the next phase, local teams will use the multibeam system on a local vessel to survey St Helena's coastal waters. Enabling local teams to use and maintain this technology is an important step towards building a sustainable hydrographic capability in St Helena.
Devlin Yon, Head of Geomatic Services, St Helena Government, commented on the importance of this type of international collaboration, noting that:
Kerrie Howard, PCA Programme Manager, UKHO said:
What happens next?

This approach demonstrates the UKHO’s ongoing commitment to support its partners globally to strengthen their hydrographic capabilities. It also signals a change in how we support our partners, focusing on enabling and empowering our partners to develop their data collection capabilities.

The UKHO will continue to work with St Helena and its partners, to ensure the data collected meets international hydrographic standards (IHO S-44) and UKHO’s data requirements for producing trusted products and services. While St Helena was the first beneficiary of equipment from UKHO’s HELP, the pool is currently being expanded to support more UK Overseas Territories and UKHO partner nations. As a global leader, the UKHO is proud to support nations across the globe to provide access to equipment that may not otherwise be accessible and empower local hydrographers to undertake the surveys of their own waters.

Based on feedback from the hydrographic community in developing countries which the UKHO supports by providing charting services, the UKHO anticipates that the HELP will expand further in years to come to meet the demand. By providing our partners the skills and access to the equipment needed, UKHO aims to increase the quantity of modern data supplied by its partners for vital ports and to enable the development of the next generation of S-100 products.

title: There is no such thing as a typical Fast Streamer
authors: Olviya Silvary, Fast Stream Data Analyst

content.content: I almost ruled myself out

When I graduated with a degree in English Language and Literature, I had no idea what to do next, and a lot of anxiety around that decision. When I was accepted onto the Digital Fast Stream, I had to think carefully whether it was the right fit for me.
Looking back, I realise I nearly ruled myself out because I had an idea in my head of what a "typical" Fast Streamer looked like. The truth is, there isn't one.

The Fast Stream is a Civil Service development programme that accelerates careers through a series of postings across different government departments. For me, the Digital Fast Stream has not only exposed me to exciting and varied opportunities, but it has also sharpened my focus on my future career. Whoever you are, read on to find out why it could do the same for you, even if you don’t have a technical background.
Jumping into the deep end

I don't usually deal well with change, so knowing I had only 12 months in each posting to assimilate into the team and wider department was incredibly daunting. I'd also never had a classic office job before. I had only worked in retail and community outreach, so I was often on the go. Sitting in an office and meeting my team on a laptop screen was a real change and a real challenge in some ways.

However, my team in the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) is a fantastic, welcoming group of people. I'll be the first to say I am a chronic oversharer. My cheery morning greetings certainly took some people by surprise, but I settled in quickly. The Digital, Data and Technology (DDaT) directorate functions fluidly. It's common for people to move between professions and teams, with an emphasis on Learning and Development.
This aligns well with the purpose of the Fast Stream, which emphasises professional and personal development. The Fast Stream journey is not just about depth of learning, but variety of exposure.
The Digital Fast Stream: who is it for?
Another reason to be daunted by joining the Digital Fast Stream was that I had no data experience coming into the role. Sure, I was keen to learn, but how far would that take me?
This is not uncommon in the Fast Stream. There were many people coming into the graduate scheme from a completely different career, like 2nd year Digital and Cyber Fast Streamer Collette Ovenseri:

The Fast Stream is often thought of as a graduate scheme, but the 2025 recruitment data tells a different story. Last year 35% of successful applicants were over 23, suggesting a significant number of people on the scheme did not join straight from their undergraduate degree.

Girish Joshi, a Data Analyst and another first-year Fast Streamer in my team, previously created hot sauces and worked as a cruise ship chef. He has shown me definitively that the Fast Stream is not just for graduates:

A lot of people do also assume that it is just for people who have never worked in the Civil Service before. The scheme also accepts existing Civil Servants, for whom the degree requirements are waived. Those already working in the Civil Service may be surprised to hear that the Fast Stream still offers new experiences, opportunities and perspectives. Steve Corder, a Senior Product Manager, shares his experience.
You can make a difference as a Fast Streamer

Over the past year, I have not just contributed to my team but integrated into it. I've helped run the Data Challenge and worked on a wide variety of projects with stakeholders across government. Soon I will help welcome the next cohort of Fast Streamers at Base Camp. Andy Palmer, BIST's Senior Capability Manager says:

While it can be intimidating joining a programme like the Fast Stream, remember that the Civil Service benefits from our perspectives, just as much as we benefit from the experience. As Andy says, “we're stronger for the diversity of experiences Fast Streamers bring”.
Looking ahead

The Fast Stream doesn’t just teach digital skills, it builds flexibility and resilience. Fast Stream graduate and Senior Content Designer, Mei Mei Loh explains how that prepares Fast Streamers for future roles:

I'm not quite sure where the future will take me, but right now, I want to be fulfilled. I want a career where I am constantly adapting to new things, to be challenged on what I know and don't know, and to always keep learning. I've never been very good at standing still, and that's something the government doesn’t do either. I don't want to necessarily be the best there is, but someone who is always pushing for better. What better place for that than the Civil Service?
Is the Fast Stream right for you?

As October (and my next placement) approaches, I don't think I will ever be rid of the fear of the unknown. What I have learned from the Fast Stream, however, is that moving between teams and diving into unfamiliar environments gives you opportunities to grow.
If you are:
Then my advice to you is don’t rule yourself out.
Explore the Digital scheme. Applications open in October, and hopefully we'll see you in DDaT next autumn!
